pacman::p_load(tidyverse,   # data wrangling and plots

# One framework, two kinds of distance

| | Phylogenetic | Spatial |
|---|---|---|
| Unit | species | site / population |
| Distance | branch length (patristic distance) | geographic distance (km) |
| Correlation | Brownian motion: shared branch length (`vcv(tree, corr = TRUE)`); or decaying with distance | decays with distance, e.g., exponential $\rho(d) = e^{-d/\phi}$ |
| `metafor` | `R = list(phylo = A)` or `struct = "SPEXP"` + `dist =` | `struct = "SPEXP"` (or `"SPGAU"`, ...) + `dist =` |
| `brms` | `(1 | gr(phylo, cov = A))` | `gp(x, y)` or `(1 | gr(site, cov = Sigma))` |

```{r}
#| label: fig-decay
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Exponential and Gaussian correlation functions for a range parameter of 300 (km or branch-length units). The range, φ, is the distance at which the correlation of an exponential function has fallen to e⁻¹ ≈ 0.37."
#| fig-height: 3.5
# Correlation at each distance for a range parameter of 300
decay <- tibble(d = seq(0, 1500, by = 5)) %>%
  mutate(`Exponential (SPEXP)` = exp(-d / 300),
         `Gaussian (SPGAU)`    = exp(-(d / 300)^2)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -d, names_to = "structure", values_to = "correlation")

ggplot(decay, aes(x = d, y = correlation, colour = structure)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = exp(-1), linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 300, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(pal[c("red", "dark")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Distance", y = "Correlation between random effects")
```

---

# 1. Phylogenetic meta-analysis: BM vs an exponential (OU-like) model

In the [non-independence tutorial](../models/non-independence.qmd), we assumed **Brownian motion** (BM): the correlation between two species equals their proportion of shared history. An alternative lets correlation decay **exponentially** with patristic distance, $\rho = e^{-d/\phi}$, which corresponds to an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process with $\alpha = 1/\phi$ [@Mizuno2026]. We compare them using the dive data set from the [meta-regression tutorial](meta-regression.qmd).

```{r}
#| label: phylo-data
# 1. Download the data and tidy the species names (as in the meta-regression tutorial)
dive <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/essierodgers/diving-meta-analysis/master/data/contrast_lab_dataset.csv")

dive$species <- str_trim(dive$species)
dive$species <- str_replace_all(dive$species, " ", "_")
dive$species <- str_replace(dive$species, "Trachemys_scripta_elegans", "Trachemys_scripta")

dive$phylo <- dive$species      # copy of species for the phylogenetic random effect
dive$es_ID <- 1:nrow(dive)      # effect size ID
dive$const <- 1                 # a single 'group' that contains every row (needed for SPEXP)

# 2. Calculate lnRR_Q10 and its sampling variance
lnRR_Q10 <- function(t1, t2, r1, r2, sd1, sd2, n1, n2) {
  scale_10   <- 10 / (t2 - t1)
  lnRR_Q10   <- scale_10 * log(r2 / r1)
  V_lnRR_Q10 <- scale_10^2 * (sd1^2 / (n1 * r1^2) + sd2^2 / (n2 * r2^2))
  data.frame(lnRR_Q10, V_lnRR_Q10)
}

q10_es <- lnRR_Q10(t1  = dive$t1,      t2  = dive$t2,
                   r1  = dive$mean_t1, r2  = dive$mean_t2,
                   sd1 = dive$sd_t1,   sd2 = dive$sd_t2,
                   n1  = dive$n_t1,    n2  = dive$n_t2)

dive <- cbind(dive, q10_es)

# 3. Phylogeny
tree <- read.tree("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/essierodgers/diving-meta-analysis/master/data/phylo_lab.nwk")
tree <- keep.tip(tree, unique(dive$species))

A       <- vcv(tree, corr = TRUE)       # Brownian motion correlation matrix
D_phylo <- cophenetic.phylo(tree)       # patristic distances (2 x divergence time, Mya)

# 4a. Brownian motion model
phylo_bm <- rma.mv(yi = lnRR_Q10,
                   V = V_lnRR_Q10,
                   random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                                 ~ 1 | es_ID,
                                 ~ 1 | phylo),
                   R = list(phylo = A),           # BM correlation matrix
                   data = dive)

# 4b. Exponential decay of the correlation with patristic distance
phylo_exp <- rma.mv(yi = lnRR_Q10,
                    V = V_lnRR_Q10,
                    random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                                  ~ 1 | es_ID,
                                  ~ phylo | const),   # species effects correlated by distance
                    struct = "SPEXP",                 # exponential decay
                    dist = list(phylo = D_phylo),     # the distance matrix to use
                    data = dive)

summary(phylo_exp)

# 5. Compare the two models
phylo_compare <- data.frame(
  model    = c("Brownian motion", "Exponential (OU-like)"),
  estimate = c(phylo_bm$b[1],  phylo_exp$b[1]),
  ci_lb    = c(phylo_bm$ci.lb, phylo_exp$ci.lb),
  ci_ub    = c(phylo_bm$ci.ub, phylo_exp$ci.ub),
  AIC      = c(AIC(phylo_bm),  AIC(phylo_exp))
)

phylo_compare
```

**Interpretation.** `rho` is the range on the branch-length scale (here, twice the divergence time in Mya). A lower AIC indicates a better *relative* fit among the candidate covariance structures – it is **not** evidence that traits evolved by an OU process [@Mizuno2026]. In practice, check whether the pooled mean is robust to the choice; here both models give very similar estimates.

# 2. Spatial meta-analysis

## Data: plasticity of heat tolerance across eastern Australia

`sim_spatial_arr.csv` contains **simulated** acclimation response ratios (ARR; change in CTmax per °C of acclimation temperature) for 40 populations of a widespread skink, from 17 studies. Populations close to each other experience similar climates and exchange genes, so their ARRs may be **spatially autocorrelated** beyond what latitude alone explains.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-data
# Read the simulated data from the data folder
arr_dat <- read.csv(here::here("data", "sim_spatial_arr.csv"))

arr_dat$es_ID   <- 1:nrow(arr_dat)                                # effect size ID
arr_dat$site_ID <- factor(arr_dat$site_ID)                        # site as a factor
arr_dat$const   <- 1                                              # one group for SPEXP
arr_dat$lat_c   <- arr_dat$latitude - mean(arr_dat$latitude)      # centred latitude

head(arr_dat)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Locations of the 40 populations, coloured by ARR. Nearby populations tend to have similar values."
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-width: 6
ggplot(arr_dat, aes(x = longitude, y = latitude, colour = ARR)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5) +
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#1A2533", high = "#e12744") +   # navy (low) to red (high)
  labs(x = "Longitude (°E)", y = "Latitude (°N; negative = south)") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

## From coordinates to a distance matrix

We need distances in kilometres between all pairs of sites, in the **same order as the levels** of `site_ID`. For global data, use ellipsoidal geodesic distances (e.g., `geosphere::distm(..., fun = distGeo)`); here, a great-circle (haversine) formula written in base R is accurate enough:

```{r}
#| label: dist
# gc_dist_km(): great-circle distance matrix (km) from longitude/latitude in decimal degrees
# (haversine formula: the shortest distance over the Earth's surface)
gc_dist_km <- function(lon, lat, labels) {
  # conversion factor from degrees to radians (trig functions in R use radians)
  rad <- pi / 180
  # outer() calls the function below for every pair of sites (i, j)
  # and returns a k x k matrix of distances
  D <- outer(seq_along(lon), seq_along(lon), function(i, j) {
    # difference in latitude and longitude between sites i and j, in radians
    dlat <- (lat[j] - lat[i]) * rad
    dlon <- (lon[j] - lon[i]) * rad
    # haversine term: combines the north-south and east-west separation,
    # shrinking the east-west part by cos(latitude) because meridians converge at the poles
    a <- sin(dlat / 2)^2 + cos(lat[i] * rad) * cos(lat[j] * rad) * sin(dlon / 2)^2
    # central angle (2 * asin(sqrt(a))) times the Earth's mean radius (6371 km) = distance in km;
    # pmin(1, ...) guards against rounding pushing sqrt(a) just above 1, where asin() returns NaN
    2 * 6371 * asin(pmin(1, sqrt(a)))
  })
  # name the rows and columns with the site labels so sites can be looked up by name
  dimnames(D) <- list(labels, labels)
  D
}

# one row per site with its coordinates, sorted by site_ID so that the order
# matches the factor levels of site_ID used in the model
sites <- arr_dat %>%
  distinct(site_ID, longitude, latitude) %>%
  arrange(site_ID)

# build the site-by-site distance matrix (km)
D_km <- gc_dist_km(lon = sites$longitude,
                   lat = sites$latitude,
                   labels = as.character(sites$site_ID))

# safety check: rma.mv() matches rows of the distance matrix to the levels of site_ID
# by position, so stop with an error if the order differs
stopifnot(identical(rownames(D_km), levels(arr_dat$site_ID)))   # order must match!

# preview the distances (km, rounded) between the first four sites
round(D_km[1:4, 1:4])
```

## Is there spatial signal?

A quick diagnostic: after removing the latitudinal trend, do pairs of nearby populations have more similar residuals than distant pairs?

```{r}
#| label: fig-correlogram
#| fig-cap: "Similarity of residual ARR (product of standardised residuals from a non-spatial model) against distance between populations. Positive values at short distances indicate spatial autocorrelation."
#| fig-height: 3.4

# 1. Fit a non-spatial model with latitude as a moderator
mod_nonspatial <- rma.mv(yi = ARR,
                         V = V_ARR,
                         mods = ~ lat_c,
                         random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                                       ~ 1 | es_ID),
                         data = arr_dat)

# 2. Standardised residuals: what is left after removing the latitudinal trend
res_std <- rstandard(mod_nonspatial)$z

# 3. Every pair of effect sizes (i, j), counting each pair once
pairs <- expand_grid(i = 1:nrow(arr_dat), j = 1:nrow(arr_dat)) %>%
  filter(i < j)

# Look up the distance between the two sites of each pair (by site name)
site_i <- as.character(arr_dat$site_ID[pairs$i])
site_j <- as.character(arr_dat$site_ID[pairs$j])
pairs$dist <- D_km[cbind(site_i, site_j)]

# Similarity: positive when both residuals are on the same side of the trend
pairs$similarity <- res_std[pairs$i] * res_std[pairs$j]

# 4. Average similarity within distance bins
#    (narrower bins at short distances, where spatial correlation is strongest)
correlogram <- pairs %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(dist, breaks = c(0, 150, 300, 500, 800, 1200, 1800, 2600))) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>%
  summarise(dist = mean(dist),
            similarity = mean(similarity),
            n = n())

ggplot(correlogram, aes(x = dist, y = similarity)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(colour = pal["red"]) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = pal["red"]) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Distance between populations (km)", y = "Mean residual similarity")
```

## Fitting the spatial model

Following @Mizuno2026, we compare three random-effects structures, each with latitude as a moderator:

```{r}
#| label: spatial-models
# 1. Unstructured: study and effect size random effects only
sp_unstr <- rma.mv(yi = ARR,
                   V = V_ARR,
                   mods = ~ lat_c,
                   random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                                 ~ 1 | es_ID),
                   test = "t",
                   data = arr_dat)

# 2. Combined: + a spatially correlated site effect (exponential decay with distance)
sp_comb <- rma.mv(yi = ARR,
                  V = V_ARR,
                  mods = ~ lat_c,
                  random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                                ~ 1 | es_ID,
                                ~ site_ID | const),   # spatial term indexed by site
                  struct = "SPEXP",                   # exponential correlation function
                  dist = list(site_ID = D_km),        # our distance matrix (km)
                  test = "t",
                  data = arr_dat)

summary(sp_comb)

# 3. The same model, using metafor's built-in great-circle distances from the coordinates
sp_gcd <- rma.mv(yi = ARR,
                 V = V_ARR,
                 mods = ~ lat_c,
                 random = list(~ 1 | study_ID,
                               ~ 1 | es_ID,
                               ~ longitude + latitude | const),
                 struct = "SPEXP",
                 dist = "gcd",                         # great-circle distance
                 test = "t",
                 data = arr_dat)

# The estimated range (km) is the same either way
c(rho_own_matrix = sp_comb$rho, rho_gcd = sp_gcd$rho)
```

```{r}
#| label: spatial-compare
# Compare the latitude slope, its SE and the model fit
fitstats_tbl <- data.frame(
  model          = c("Unstructured", "Combined (spatial)"),
  latitude_slope = c(sp_unstr$b[2],  sp_comb$b[2]),
  se_slope       = c(sp_unstr$se[2], sp_comb$se[2]),
  AIC            = c(AIC(sp_unstr),  AIC(sp_comb)),
  range_km       = c(NA,             sp_comb$rho)
)

fitstats_tbl

# Likelihood-ratio test of the spatial term
anova(sp_comb, sp_unstr)
```

## Comparing the non-spatial and spatial models visually

```{r}
#| label: fig-spatial-compare
#| fig-cap: "Non-spatial (unstructured) vs spatial (exponential SPEXP) models. (A) Intercept (ARR at the mean latitude) and latitude slope with 95% CIs. (B) Fitted latitudinal trend with 95% confidence bands; points are populations, sized by precision. (C) Variance components: the spatial model moves part of the heterogeneity from the study and effect-size levels into a spatially structured term."
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-width: 10
# Colours for the two models
model_cols <- c("Non-spatial" = "#1A2533", "Spatial (SPEXP)" = "#e12744")

# (A) Fixed effects: intercept and latitude slope from each model -----------
coef_tbl <- data.frame(
  model    = rep(c("Non-spatial", "Spatial (SPEXP)"), each = 2),
  term     = rep(c("Intercept (ARR at mean latitude)",
                   "Latitude slope (per degree north)"), times = 2),
  estimate = c(sp_unstr$b[, 1],  sp_comb$b[, 1]),
  ci_lb    = c(sp_unstr$ci.lb,   sp_comb$ci.lb),
  ci_ub    = c(sp_unstr$ci.ub,   sp_comb$ci.ub)
)

p_coef <- ggplot(coef_tbl, aes(x = estimate, y = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = ci_lb, xmax = ci_ub),
                width = 0.2, orientation = "y", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  facet_wrap(~ term, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Estimate (95% CI)", y = NULL, title = "A  Fixed effects")

# (B) Fitted latitudinal trend from each model -------------------------------

# 100 latitudes across the observed range (and the centred version for the model)
lat_grid <- data.frame(latitude = seq(min(arr_dat$latitude), max(arr_dat$latitude),
                                      length.out = 100))
lat_grid$lat_c <- lat_grid$latitude - mean(arr_dat$latitude)

# Predictions (with 95% CIs) from each model
pred_unstr <- as.data.frame(predict(sp_unstr, newmods = lat_grid$lat_c))
pred_unstr$model    <- "Non-spatial"
pred_unstr$latitude <- lat_grid$latitude

pred_comb <- as.data.frame(predict(sp_comb, newmods = lat_grid$lat_c))
pred_comb$model    <- "Spatial (SPEXP)"
pred_comb$latitude <- lat_grid$latitude

pred_tbl <- bind_rows(pred_unstr, pred_comb)

p_trend <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = arr_dat, aes(x = latitude, y = ARR, size = 1 / sqrt(V_ARR)),
             colour = "grey45", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(data = pred_tbl, aes(x = latitude, ymin = ci.lb, ymax = ci.ub, fill = model),
              alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(data = pred_tbl, aes(x = latitude, y = pred, colour = model),
            linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = model_cols, name = NULL) +
  guides(size = "none") +
  labs(x = "Latitude (°N; negative = south)", y = "ARR (°C per °C)",
       title = "B  Fitted latitudinal trend")

# (C) Variance components of each model --------------------------------------
vc_tbl <- data.frame(
  model     = rep(c("Non-spatial", "Spatial (SPEXP)"), each = 3),
  component = rep(c("Study", "Effect size", "Spatial (site)"), times = 2),
  variance  = c(sp_unstr$sigma2, 0,               # the non-spatial model has no spatial term
                sp_comb$sigma2,  sp_comb$tau2)
)
vc_tbl$component <- factor(vc_tbl$component,
                           levels = c("Study", "Effect size", "Spatial (site)"))

p_vc <- ggplot(vc_tbl, aes(x = model, y = variance, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(pal[c("dark", "pink", "red")]), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Variance", title = "C  Variance components")

# Combine the three panels with patchwork
p_coef / (p_trend + p_vc + plot_layout(widths = c(1.6, 1))) +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.3))
```

**What the figure shows**

- **Panel A:** the latitude slope is `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_unstr$b[2])` in the non-spatial model and `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$b[2])` in the spatial model, and its standard error `r if_else(sp_comb$se[2] > sp_unstr$se[2], "increases", "decreases")` from `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_unstr$se[2])` to `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$se[2])`. Once nearby populations are allowed to resemble each other, they no longer count as fully independent replicates of the latitude effect.
- **Panel B:** both models describe the same latitudinal trend. The spatial model's confidence band is `r if_else(mean(pred_tbl$ci.ub[pred_tbl$model == "Spatial (SPEXP)"] - pred_tbl$ci.lb[pred_tbl$model == "Spatial (SPEXP)"]) > mean(pred_tbl$ci.ub[pred_tbl$model == "Non-spatial"] - pred_tbl$ci.lb[pred_tbl$model == "Non-spatial"]), "wider", "narrower")`, reflecting the different estimate of independent information.
- **Panel C:** total heterogeneity is similar in the two models (`r sprintf("%.4f", sum(sp_unstr$sigma2))` vs `r sprintf("%.4f", sum(sp_comb$sigma2) + sp_comb$tau2)`), but it is partitioned differently. Most of what the non-spatial model treats as independent variation among effect sizes is attributed by the spatial model to a spatially structured site effect (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * sp_comb$tau2 / (sum(sp_comb$sigma2) + sp_comb$tau2))`% of the total). In other words, much of the 'unexplained' variation is shared by neighbouring populations.

## Interpreting

- `tau^2` is the spatial variance and `rho` the **range** (km): the estimated spatial correlation falls to 0.37 at ~`r round(sp_comb$rho)` km (the simulation used 300 km).
- Including the spatial term changes the standard error of the latitude slope, because nearby populations no longer count as fully independent replicates of the latitude effect.
- Spatial range parameters are often **weakly identified**: profile the likelihood (`profile(sp_comb, tau2 = 1)`), try different starting values, and report sensitivity to the correlation function (`"SPGAU"`, `"SPSPH"`) [@Mizuno2026].

```{r}
#| label: fig-fitted-decay
#| fig-cap: "Estimated spatial correlation between population effects as a function of distance (exponential model), compared with the value used to simulate the data."
#| fig-height: 3
# Estimated vs true spatial correlation at each distance
fitted_decay <- tibble(d = 0:1500) %>%
  mutate(Estimated = exp(-d / sp_comb$rho),
         `True (simulation)` = exp(-d / 300)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -d, names_to = "curve", values_to = "correlation")

ggplot(fitted_decay, aes(x = d, y = correlation, linetype = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = pal["red"]) +
  labs(x = "Distance (km)", y = "Spatial correlation", linetype = NULL)
```

## brms and glmmTMB versions

::: {.panel-tabset}
## brms (Gaussian process)
```{r}
#| eval: false
library(brms)
# Project coordinates to km on a local plane (adequate for regional data)
arr_dat$x_km <- (arr_dat$longitude - mean(arr_dat$longitude)) * 111.32 * cos(mean(arr_dat$latitude) * pi / 180)
arr_dat$y_km <- (arr_dat$latitude - mean(arr_dat$latitude)) * 110.57

sp_brms <- brm(
  bf(ARR | se(sqrt(V_ARR), sigma = TRUE) ~ lat_c + (1 | study_ID) +
       gp(x_km, y_km, cov = "exponential", scale = FALSE)),   # exponential GP over space
  data = arr_dat, family = gaussian(),
  prior = c(prior(normal(0, 1), class = "Intercept"),
            prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "sd"),
            prior(student_t(3, 0, 0.5), class = "sdgp"),
            prior(lognormal(log(300), 1), class = "lscale")),   # weakly informative range (km)
  chains = 4, cores = 4, iter = 4000, warmup = 2000, seed = 2026,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99), file = here::here("brms_fits", "sp_brms"))
```

## brms (fixed spatial matrix)
```{r}
#| eval: false
# If you prefer a fixed correlation matrix (e.g., with the range taken from the metafor fit)
Sigma <- exp(-D_km / 300)
sp_brms_fixed <- brm(
  ARR | se(sqrt(V_ARR)) ~ lat_c + (1 | study_ID) + (1 | es_ID) + (1 | gr(site_ID, cov = Sigma)),
  data = arr_dat, data2 = list(Sigma = Sigma), chains = 4, cores = 4)
```
:::

# Your turn

1. Refit `sp_comb` with `struct = "SPGAU"`. Compare AIC and the estimated range.
2. Remove `lat_c` from the spatial model. What happens to the spatial variance, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
```{r}
#| label: your-turn-answers

# 1. Gaussian instead of exponential correlation function
sp_gau <- update(sp_comb, struct = "SPGAU")

c(AIC_exp = AIC(sp_comb), AIC_gau = AIC(sp_gau))   # model fit
c(rho_exp = sp_comb$rho,  rho_gau = sp_gau$rho)    # estimated range (km)

# 2. Remove latitude from the spatial model
sp_nolat <- update(sp_comb, mods = ~ 1)

c(spatial_var_with_lat = sp_comb$tau2, spatial_var_without_lat = sp_nolat$tau2)
```
Without the latitude moderator, the broad-scale latitudinal gradient is absorbed by the spatial random effect, inflating the spatial variance and range. Spatial random effects and spatially structured moderators compete for the same signal.
:::

# Writing it up

::: {.writeup}
To account for spatial non-independence among populations, we included a spatially structured random effect with an exponential correlation function of great-circle distance between sites (`struct = "SPEXP"` in metafor), alongside random effects for study and effect size [@Mizuno2026]. Acclimation capacity `r if_else(sp_comb$b[2] > 0, "increased", "decreased")` towards the tropics (slope = `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$b[2])` °C °C⁻¹ per degree of latitude northwards, 95% CI `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$ci.lb[2])` to `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$ci.ub[2])`). Residual spatial autocorrelation was estimated with a range of `r round(sp_comb$rho)` km (spatial variance = `r sprintf("%.4f", sp_comb$tau2)`), and the spatial model `r if_else(AIC(sp_comb) - AIC(sp_unstr) < -2, "was clearly preferred over", "fitted the data similarly to")` the non-spatial model (ΔAIC = `r sprintf("%.1f", AIC(sp_comb) - AIC(sp_unstr))`; likelihood-ratio test *p* `r fmt_p(anova(sp_comb, sp_unstr)$pval)`). We therefore report the spatial model as a sensitivity analysis showing that the latitudinal trend is robust to spatial autocorrelation.
:::
